_note: The five paid flowers, generated with create_image_pixen at genuinely low resolution and shipped at native size — the browser upscales them with image-rendering: pixelated, so a 36x48 bloom draws at 92px with art pixels about two screen pixels across. That is the whole point: the first attempt generated the same flowers at the sunflower's 172x244 and they came back as smooth little illustrations that read as a different medium beside it, because a large canvas buys detail rather than pixels. Resolution is the style. Pixen is used rather than pixflux because it holds up better at these sizes and, unlike a forced palette, returns real transparency. The sunflower is older hand-kept art and has no job here.
constraints: Pixen requires sides that are multiples of 4, and a square canvas if either side is under 32 — which is why the bud is 32x44 rather than the 24x36 its proportions wanted.

daisy-bloom@seed11.why: Head about a fifth of the canvas, so at the 92px it ships at the flower read as a white dot on a stick. The fix was in the prompt, not the seed: asking for the head to fill the top half of the image.

lily-bloom@seed11.why: Same problem as the daisy, worse — a lily's petals are thin, so a small head lost them entirely at display size.

daisy-bloom@palette.why: The white-petalled flowers cannot use a forced palette. A palette makes the generator return the art flattened onto its lightest colour instead of transparency, and on the daisy and the lily that lightest colour IS the petal — so keying the backdrop took the petals with it and left a yellow disc floating on a stem. Both are generated palette-free instead, with the greens named in the prompt; the backdrop then comes back a pale green the petals never use, and keys cleanly.

lily-bloom@palette.why: Same as the daisy: cream petals the same colour as the forced backdrop, so keying ate holes through them.

lily-bloom@white.why: A white lily on light-green grass is nearly all highlight: at 92px its petals lost their edges and the whole flower read as a pale smudge, with a broken orange outline. Every other species carries a colour that holds at display size, so the lily became a pink stargazer — still the most-planted lily there is, and it survives the downscale.

rose-sprout@wide.why: An attempt to widen the seedling to the sunflower sprout's chunkier proportions, by asking for big leaves spreading left and right. It drew the leaves genuinely detached — floating either side of a stemless mound of soil — and the clean-up then binned them as strays. The narrower first batch is kept: it is a little slighter than the sunflower's seedling, but it is a plant.

rose-bud@seed11.why: Drew one leaf detached from a hair-thin stem; the clean-up binned the leaf as a stray and what shipped was a bud on a bare wire. Re-prompted for a thick stem and a leaf either side.

lily-bud@cream.why: Cream tips, drawn against the white lily this species used to be. Once the bloom became a pink stargazer the bud had to follow, or a garden changed colour as it grew.

ALL@highres.why: Every sprite, generated at the sunflower's own canvas sizes (bloom 172x244, bud 136x220, sprout 108x76) on the theory that matching the canvas would match the apparent pixel size. It does not. The sunflower's canvas holds chunky blocks; a fresh generation at that size holds fine detail, and then gets downscaled 2.3x to display, which mushes it. Beside the sunflower they read as smooth illustrations rather than pixel art. Regenerated small. The old jobs, palettes and their own rejects are recorded in git history at c2595fd.

tulip-sprout@seed23.why: Leaves drooping like a dying plant, with a blue fringe around them.

lily-sprout@seed41.why: Came out small and yellow — reads as a seedling that is already failing.

daisy-bud@seed11.why: A green dome with white petals dangling under it; read as a lampshade rather than a bud about to open.

tulip-sprout@seed67.why: Leggy — four leaves up a tall stem, a young plant rather than a seedling just out of the ground.

lily-sprout@seed71.why: Soil came out near-black blue, and one leaf pale yellow.

daisy-bud@seed67.why: A mottled blue-green ball on a stalk — a thistle, not a daisy about to open.

_sprout_note: Seedlings are where the prompt matters most and the species matters least: at 34px a rose seedling and a lily seedling are the same two leaves. Asking for 'exactly two seed leaves in a V shape' is what reliably produces a sprout rather than a leggy young plant, and naming brown soil explicitly stops the mound coming back near-black blue.
